newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand slipped, regained its composure and strode firmer before retracing its steps to trade little changed on Tuesday as South Africa allowed local individuals to invest offshore for the first time since 1961.

After initially weakening to a day's low of 4.5425 against the dollar, the rand strengthened to 4.5235 bid by early afternoon before slipping back to 4.5285/5315 by 1405 GMT from 4.5280/5310 late on Monday.

On Tuesday, exchange controls were lifted on South African individuals allowing them to invest up to 200,000 rand offshore -- a move which had triggered dollar demand from local banks and importers in recent weeks amid concerns that the rand would weaken post-July 1.
Dealers said the rand was initially ruffled on Tuesday by an order to buy dollars, said by one trader to have been a speculative position taken by a local exporter.
The lead was taken up by London banks who took speculative positions by buying dollars. But their efforts were thwarted by a market which dealers said was generally long dollars.
Both local and offshore players who had accumulated dollars ahead of the easing also cut their positions, as the expected demand failed to materialise.
"I think the day went as the market expected," a rand trader said. "It weakened at first and when it couldn't push higher people started offloading their longs."
Analysts said that from an exchange control point of view, the day had been a non-event.
"Its been exceptionally quiet. A lot of enquiries but a non-event," said Autrey Wilke, general manager of international treasury trading at Absa Bank.
Dealers said that with July 1 now out of the way, the rand was expected to trade in a range of between 4.52 to 4.55 against the dollar.

Most local banks appeared to be well positioned for any demand the market might see in the weeks ahead, while dealers said offshore players appeared content to continue investing in local bonds and equities.
Bonds in particular benefited from the rand's sturdiness on the day, firming over 10 basis points on the back of both local and offshore buying.
The key R150 stock was last quoted at 14.26 percent from 14.36 percent on Monday after touching a day's low of 14.235 percent earlier.
Dealers said yields were driven lower by both local and offshore buying before running into resistance at the day's low from local institutional profit-taking.
"It's generally been very quiet but the market is really happy with the way the market handled itself," a trader said.
He added that the market was now setting its sites on the gold and foreign exchange reserves data, due for release at 1800 GMT, for fresh fuel to help the market lower.
Economists expect reserve to rise to anything between 23 and 28 billion rand in June, with consensus at 24.68 billion rand from 21.8 billion rand in May.
"If the figure is at the higher end of the range I think we can go lower," a trader said.

On the money market, short-term rates dipped to between 14.75 and 14.80 percent offered from 14.85 percent on Monday, while the 90-day BA rate was quoted at between 15.40 and 15.20 percent from between 15.40 and 15.25 percent before.
The Reserve Bank quoted the money market shortage lower at 5.092 billion rand on Monday from 5.376 billion rand on Saturday.
Bond Exchange figures showed foreigners were net buyers of 359.27 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Monday after selling 267.89 million rand's worth on Friday.
Nominal cumulative volumes on the bond market on Monday were 5.36 billion rand on Monday from 9.48 billion rand on Friday.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003
